## Department of Homeland Security
• 8 CFR Part 207
• [CIS No. 2856-26; DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0397]
( printed page 65077)
## AGENCY:
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
## ACTION:
Interim final rule.
## SUMMARY:

This interim final rule (IFR) amends Department of Homeland Security (DHS) regulations to expedite termination of refugee status when DHS determines an alien was not a refugee within the meaning of section 101(a)(42) of the Immigration and Nationality Act at the time of admission to the United States. The response period to a Notice of Intent to Terminate (NOIT) is reduced from thirty to ten days. These changes aim to restore integrity to the immigration system, mitigate risks to national security and public safety, and prevent fraud and exploitation.
## DATES:

This IFR is effective on October 14, 2026. Written comments and related materials must be submitted on or before November 13, 2026. The electronic Federal Docket Management System will accept comments prior to midnight Eastern Time at the end of that day.
## ADDRESSES:

You may submit comments on the entirety of this rulemaking package, identified by DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0397, through the Federal eRulemaking Portal: https://www.regulations.gov . Follow the website instructions for submitting comments.

Comments must be submitted in English, or an English translation must be provided. Comments that will provide the most assistance to USCIS in implementing these changes will reference a specific portion of the Interim Final Rule, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include data, information, or authority that support such recommended change. Comments submitted in a manner other than the one listed above, including emails or letters sent to DHS or USCIS officials, will not be considered comments on the Interim Final Rule and may not receive a response from DHS. Please note that DHS and USCIS cannot accept any comments that are hand-delivered or couriered. In addition, USCIS cannot accept comments contained on any form of digital media storage devices, such as CDs/DVDs and USB drives. USCIS is also not accepting mailed comments at this time. If you cannot submit your comment by using https://www.regulations.gov , please contact the Regulatory Coordination Division, Office of Policy and Strategy, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Department of Homeland Security, by telephone at (240) 721-3000 for alternate instructions.
## FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

Security, Public Safety, and Global Vetting Division (SPSG), Office of Policy & Strategy, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), DHS, 5900 Capital Gateway Drive, Camp Springs, MD 20746; telephone (240) 721-3000. Individuals with hearing or speech impairments may access the telephone number above via TTY by calling the toll-free Federal Information Relay Service at 711.

## I. Public Participation
DHS invites all interested parties to participate in this rulemaking by submitting written data, views, comments and arguments on all aspects
( printed page 65078)

of this IFR. DHS also invites comments that relate to the economic, environmental, or federalism effects that might result from this IFR. Comments must be submitted in English, or an English translation must be provided. Comments that will provide the most assistance to USCIS in implementing these changes will reference a specific portion of the IFR, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include data, information, or authority that support such recommended change. Comments submitted in a manner other than the one listed above, including emails or letters sent to DHS or USCIS officials, will not be considered comments on the IFR and may not receive a response from DHS.

Instructions: If you submit a comment, you must include the agency name (U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services) and the DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0397 for this rulemaking. Regardless of the method used for submitting comments or material, all submissions will be posted, without change, to the Federal eRulemaking Portal at https://www.regulations.gov , and will include any personal information you provide. Therefore, submitting this information makes it public. You may wish to consider limiting the amount of personal information that you provide in any voluntary public comment submission you make to DHS. For additional information, please read the Privacy and Security Notice available at https://www.regulations.gov .

Docket: For access to the docket and to read background documents or comments received, go to https://www.regulations.gov , referencing DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0397. You may also sign up for email alerts on the online docket to be notified when comments are posted or a final rule is published.
## II. Executive Summary
## A. Purpose of the Regulatory Action

The purpose of this rulemaking is to shorten the termination notice period in order to mitigate potential risks posed by aliens admitted to the United States as refugees when, in fact, they were not eligible for refugee classification at the time of admission. Those who are improperly admitted may not have their identity fully confirmed and vetted due to an incomplete record, and as such pose a risk to program integrity and may pose a risk to national security and public safety. A review of refugee processing policies and procedures implemented under the Biden administration indicates an alarming erosion of integrity leading to aliens being admitted to the United States as refugees when their identities, eligibility for refugee classification, and admissibility were determined based on incomplete records. [ 1 ]

Operational guidance implemented during this period allowed officers to forgo typical lines of inquiry, sacrificing the caliber and efficacy of the refugee interview, a critical screening component of the refugee adjudication process. [ 2 ]

The priority of expediency over quality encouraged a lack of robust interviews. Certain questions to ensure that aliens were eligible for refugee status prior to admission to the United States were omitted and this increased the risk of ineligible aliens being approved for refugee classification and subsequently admitted to the United States. This is supported by a recent preliminary review of admitted refugees residing in Minnesota who were interviewed, approved, and admitted during the Biden administration. For the majority of these reviewed cases, the evidence was insufficient to establish that the principal applicant met all of the required elements of the refugee definition. [ 3 ]

The goal was to have as many refugees as practicable enter the United States to meet President Biden's ceiling for refugee admissions and in order to accomplish this, a number of requirements for ensuring a thorough examination and assessment of eligibility were reduced or removed.

This raises concerns about the integrity of the refugee program and calls into question the eligibility for refugee status of aliens admitted to the United States during this time. As detailed below in this preamble, several policy decisions were implemented that significantly reduced the integrity measures within the refugee program. These changes resulted in an increase in the number of refugee interviews conducted per officer each day, with less comprehensive elicitation of testimony from applicants. These adjustments limited the ability of refugee officers, and the U.S. government to accurately determine whether an applicant's identity was properly established, assess potential national security or public safety concerns, and verify whether the applicant met the definition of a refugee.

To protect U.S. interests and public safety, USCIS must act swiftly when DHS determines that an alien did not meet the refugee definition and was not entitled to refugee status at the time of admission. Shortening the NOIT response period enables DHS to respond rapidly to such findings. Allowing a longer notice period could provide opportunities for aliens to evade enforcement or engage in harmful activities. For example, the Fraud Detection and National Security (FDNS) Directorate investigated cases where refugees were later identified as members of armed groups or had concealed extremist affiliations. In one case, a refugee was found to have participated in human rights abuses with the Liberian Armed Forces during the Liberian Civil War. In another case, a refugee was found to have misrepresented his involvement with the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF), an armed group in Ethiopia. Social media checks indicated numerous pro-OLF activities and pro-OLF and radical violent rhetoric posted prior to his admission to the United States as a refugee. These cases demonstrate that when credible evidence of national security or public safety concerns arises after a refugee's admission, USCIS may be unable to initiate removal proceedings until the termination process is complete. Therefore, reducing the response period to ten days after issuance of a NOIT allows USCIS to address such threats more quickly and effectively, restoring integrity to the immigration system.
To be eligible for admission to the United States as a refugee, an alien must establish, among other things, that they meet the definition of “refugee” as defined in section 101(a)(42)(A) and (B)
( printed page 65079)

of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42)(A) and (B) , which includes the requirement that they are not a persecutor. When USCIS discovers after an alien's admission to the United States that they should not have been admitted because they did not meet the refugee definition and therefore the eligibility requirements for refugee classification at the time of admission, it is important to protect the integrity of the American immigration system by taking whatever steps are legally available, including ensuring that the alien is removed from the United States as quickly as possible where there is a legal basis to do so. There is an inherent risk to national security and public safety when an alien's identity has not been fully established. Therefore, the ability to streamline refugee status termination, where appropriate, contributes immediately to the safety of the American people and the integrity of the lawful U.S. immigration system.

The current notice and response process for terminating refugee status upon determination that the alien was not a refugee at the time of their admission is inefficient and compromises the security and safety of the United States. Providing 30 days to respond to a NOIT, instead of a 10-day response period, allows ineligible aliens more time to retain immigration benefits to which they are not entitled, undermining the integrity of the U.S. immigration system and national interests of the United States. Moreover, when an alien retains a status he or she is not entitled to, while also being inadequately vetted with insufficient information as to their true identity, there is a risk to American society's safety and security.
## B. Legal Authority

The Secretary of Homeland Security's (Secretary) authority for the regulatory amendment made in this IFR is found in various provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq., and the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (HSA), Public Law 107-296 , 116 Stat. 2135 (codified in part at 6 U.S.C. 101 et seq. ). Under the INA, the Secretary has authority over the admission, termination of status, removal, and adjustment of status of refugees. See, e.g., INA 207, 209, 8 U.S.C. 1157 , 1159 . [ 4 ]

Most importantly, section 207(c)(4) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(4) , allows the Secretary to terminate the refugee status of any alien and the alien's spouse or children if the Secretary determines that the alien “was not in fact a refugee . . . at the time of the alien's admission” and expressly authorizes the Secretary to issue regulations governing the procedures for such terminations. The Secretary has delegated the authority to grant refugee status and to adjust or terminate such status to USCIS. [ 5 ]

General authority for issuing this IFR is found in section 103(a) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1103(a) , which authorizes the Secretary to administer and enforce the immigration and nationality laws and establish such regulations as the Secretary deems necessary for carrying out such authority, as well as section 102 of the HSA, 6 U.S.C. 112 , which vests all of the functions of DHS in the Secretary and authorizes the Secretary to issue regulations. [ 6 ]
Additional authority for this rule is found in:

• Section 101(b)(1)(F) of the HSA, 6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(F) , which establishes as a primary mission of DHS the duty to, “ensure that the overall economic security of the United States is not diminished by efforts, activities, and programs aimed at securing the homeland;”
• Section 101(a)(42) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42) , which defines a refugee; and
• Section 451(a)(3) of the HSA, 6 U.S.C. 271(a)(3) , which confers authority on the USCIS Director to establish “policies for performing [immigration adjudication] functions.”
## C. Summary of the Regulatory Action
Through this IFR, DHS is amending 8 CFR 207.9 to change the 30-day notice-and-response period for aliens whose refugee status is terminated by USCIS to a 10-day notice-and-response period.
## D. Related Rulemakings
DHS is engaging in multiple rulemaking actions that are in various stages of development. [ 7 ]

DHS has considered and analyzed each of these rules for peripheral, overlapping, and interrelated effects on this rule and has found none, as this IFR is narrowly focused on refugee termination procedures.

DHS has also, to the extent possible, considered the effects, if any, of possible policy changes of which USCIS is aware. For example, a memorandum issued jointly by ICE and USCIS on February 18, 2026, impacting individuals with refugee status states, “the policy of USCIS and ICE regarding when, and under what circumstances, immigration officers may detain refugees who have failed to adjust to lawful permanent resident status.”  [ 8 ]

The policy changes announced in the memo relate to the statutory requirement at INA 209, 8 U.S.C. 1159 , governing the conditional admission of refugees and their adjustment of status, and provide that DHS may arrest and detain a refugee who has lived in the United States for at least one year and has not yet acquired LPR status under INA 209(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1159(a)(1) , to inspect and examine the refugee for admission as an LPR. [ 9 ]

While the policy changes are similarly aimed at protecting the public interest through vetting of aliens admitted as refugees, including vetting for national security, public safety, and fraud-related issues, the focus of this rule is on procedures in terminations cases, not the custody, arrest or detention of a refugee who has failed to adjust status.
DHS invites the public to submit comments during the 30-day comment period regarding anticipated interaction with related rules and policy changes.
## III. Background and Purpose
## A. Initial Refugee Processing

Refugee status in the United States is a highly sought after immigration benefit for displaced persons throughout the world due in part to the benefits it bestows as well as a pathway to permanent status. Resettlement to the United States through the United States Refugee Admissions Program (USRAP) is a multi-step process involving several agency partners. The U.S. Department of State (State) leads the annual
( printed page 65080)

consultations process, funds and oversees refugee resettlement activities, contracts with the non-governmental organizations that provide pre- and post-USCIS interview support, and facilitates the Priority 1 referrals to the USRAP process. After an alien is determined to have access to the USRAP, they may file a Form I-590, Registration for Classification as Refugee. [ 10 ]

Applications for refugee classification are primarily processed overseas and adjudicated by USCIS Refugee Officers who determine whether an alien meets the refugee definition and is otherwise eligible for resettlement to the United States. Under United States law, to be eligible for refugee classification an applicant must establish that he or she:
• is located outside the country of his or her nationality;  [ 11 ]
• is of special humanitarian concern to the United States;
• was persecuted or fears persecution due to race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or membership in a particular social group;
• is not firmly resettled in another country; and
• is admissible as an immigrant to the United States.

A refugee does not include anyone who ordered, incited, assisted, or otherwise participated in the persecution of any person on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion. Id. USCIS officers make a determination of eligibility for refugee classification based on the above elements of eligibility.

USCIS approval of an application for refugee classification authorizes U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to admit the alien “conditionally” as a refugee upon arrival at a U.S. port of entry within four months of the date of such approval. [ 12 ]

U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, the Office of Refugee Resettlement provides resettlement assistance, that includes employment training, English language training, cash assistance (in a manner that promotes early self-sufficiency), and job placement, to the aliens admitted as refugees to the United States.
Derivatives of the principal refugee applicant may include the spouse of a principal refugee and their unmarried children under the age of 21. [ 13 ]

Derivative family members may be included in the initial application for refugee status or petitioned for after the principal refugee's arrival to the United States. Id. For derivatives to be admitted to the United States as refugees, they must establish that they are admissible and not subject to the persecutor bar but are not required to prove that they meet the refugee definition or any of its elements, such as past persecution or a well-founded fear of future persecution.
In addition to resettlement in the United States, refugees receive employment authorization as soon as they arrive in the United States. [ 14 ]
## B. Termination of Refugee Status

The sole basis for USCIS to terminate the status of an alien conditionally admitted to the United States as a refugee is if USCIS determines that the alien did not meet the definition of a refugee at the time of admission to the United States. [ 15 ]

No other ground of termination is specified under the law. An alien who did not, in fact, meet the refugee definition at the time of admission would have been inadmissible, and once that status is terminated, will generally lack legal grounds to remain in the United States. [ 16 ]

The determination to terminate refugee status because the alien did not meet the definition of a refugee at the time of his or her admission to the United States applies solely to principal refugees and not to derivative refugees. In order to be eligible for refugee status, principal applicants must meet the requirements of the refugee definition in INA 101(a)(42), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42) , must be admissible to the United States, and must qualify under one of the designated USRAP processing priorities. [ 17 ]
USCIS may in turn terminate a derivative refugee's status if the principal's status is terminated. [ 18 ]
Refugee status can only be terminated while the alien remains in refugee status and has not yet adjusted to lawful permanent resident (LPR) status or naturalized. [ 19 ]

However, if USCIS has rescinded an alien's LPR status under INA 246, 8 U.S.C. 1156 , an alien admitted as a refugee reverts to the prior refugee status and his or her refugee status can be terminated if the basis for termination meets the statutory requirements. [ 20 ]

When USCIS determines that a principal refugee was not a refugee as defined in INA 101(a)(42), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42) , at the time of admission, USCIS initiates termination of refugee status. The former Immigration and Naturalization Service first implemented regulations governing the termination of refugee status following the enactment of the Refugee Act of 1980, and the process has remained substantively unchanged in the 45 years since then. [ 21 ]
USCIS issues a Notice of Intent to Terminate (NOIT) prior to termination. [ 22 ]

In the NOIT, USCIS outlines the specific basis or bases for the termination, such as a determination by USCIS that the harm the alien experienced or feared was not on account of a protected ground or, for example, that the alien had another nationality or legal status in another country such that they did not qualify as a refugee from the claimed country. The NOIT further informs the alien of his or her right to offer written or oral evidence in support of his or her refugee claim and in opposition to the proposed termination. Prior to this IFR, 8 CFR 207.9 provided that the alien has a 30-day period to respond to a NOIT. The preamble implementing this process did
( printed page 65081)
not explain the Immigration and Nationality Service's (INS) reasoning for the 30-day response period (as opposed to some other shorter or longer period). [ 23 ]

If the alien chooses to provide oral testimony, he or she must notify USCIS of his or her request for an additional interview so that USCIS may schedule the interview within 30 days of the date of the notice. The alien may also submit documentary evidence within 30 days from the date of the notice to the return address that is listed at the top of the notice. [ 24 ]
The NOIT makes clear that lack of a response to the notice within the time allotted results in termination of the alien's refugee status.

Finally, the NOIT states that if USCIS determines that the alien was not a refugee within the meaning of section 101(a)(42) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42) , at the time of admission, his or her refugee status and employment authorization will be terminated, and he or she will be subject to removal from the United States.

DHS typically reviews an alien's underlying refugee determination prior to the final adjudication of his or her adjustment of status to permanent residence and initiates termination when warranted. However, termination may be initiated at any time prior to adjustment if DHS determines the alien was not eligible for refugee status at the time he or she was admitted as a refugee.
There is no appeal from the termination of refugee status by USCIS. [ 25 ]
Upon termination USCIS processes the alien for removal under sections 235, 240, and 241 of the INA. [ 26 ]

USCIS may also place a person who was admitted as a refugee directly in removal proceedings, without termination of refugee status, on the basis of any applicable removal charge without the adjudication of an adjustment application. [ 27 ]
## C. Actions by the Prior Administration That Increased the Risk of Errant Refugee Admissions

Each year, the president sets the refugee ceiling, created by the Refugee Act of 1980. INA 207(a)(2), 8 U.S.C. 1157(a)(2) . During President Trump's first term he reduced the number each fiscal year (FY) (and additionally COVID-19 drastically reduced actual admissions) in order to review the program's integrity and make sure proper screening and vetting measures were in place and in order to shift resources to deal with the crisis at the U.S. southern border. [ 28 ]
During the following Biden administration; however, the Presidential Determination increased to a high not seen since the late 80s and early 90s. [ 29 ]
The refugee admission cap was repeatedly set at 125,000 from FY 2022 through FY 2025. [ 30 ]
Refugee actual admissions under the Biden administration reached its peak in FY 2024, which was 100,034 admissions—the highest in three decades. [ 31 ]

In order to reach this historically high level of refugee admissions, as evidenced by a number of updated policies and procedures, USCIS prioritized speed of processing over properly screening aliens. These changes to processing included, but were not limited to:

• discouraging officers from asking additional questions to identify potential areas of concern, particularly related to inadmissibility grounds, including security-related grounds, absent a clear indication that such a concern exists;

• allowing officers to use standardized country-of-origin information (COI) profiles for certain populations when making refugee determinations instead of eliciting testimony about the individual applicant's past harm or fears;
• rescinding the requirement to explore both past harm and a fear of future harm so long as the alien established one or the other when processing a refugee claim
• rescinding guidance on mandatory separate interviews for derivative applicants;
• for certain populations/processing locations, increasing the number of cases adjudicators were expected to interview and complete in a day to meet productivity expectations;
• decreasing the expected level of supervisory review of a refugee case file following adjudication; and

• rescinding guidance that prevented an alien from including their spouse as a derivative refugee where the marriage was informal and not valid under the law of the jurisdiction where it was celebrated. [ 32 ]
The majority of these changes impacted the quality of the refugee interview required under regulation. [ 33 ]

The main reasons officers elicit information during an interview are to: verify the identity of those present at the interview; determine whether to proceed with the interview; determine eligibility for a benefit being sought (if the interview relates to an application for a benefit); determine whether the individual being interviewed is subject to any bars or grounds of inadmissibility; evaluate the credibility; and identify whether fraud may be involved. [ 34 ]

Accordingly, the refugee interview is an instrumental component of robustly screening a refugee applicant. More truncated, less thorough interviews under the Biden administration damaged the integrity of refugee processing by hindering the officers' ability to appropriately gather sufficient information related to the aforementioned purposes of the refugee interview and to make an appropriate and legally sufficient decision. Consequently, these changes enabled ineligible aliens to exploit the refugee program to resettle in the United States,
( printed page 65082)
where they then have a path to permanent status, including citizenship.

USCIS further instructed its adjudicators that it was no longer necessary to ask additional detailed questions to identify and explore inadmissibility grounds, including security-related inadmissibility grounds, absent a clear indication of a concern. For example, per internal guidance, if an alien was transported across a border by smugglers, or an alien's home was attacked by an armed group, absent additional information in the record or in country conditions information indicating possible security-related concerns with respect to these incidents ( e.g., material support to a terrorist organization), officers were not required to follow up or explore if the individual was potentially inadmissible, or if these interactions raised other concerns. Officers were discouraged from investigating potential concerns or delving into an applicant's background or past experiences unless referral documents, such as the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) Resettlement Registration Form (RRF), explicitly noted concerns. In other words, officers were discouraged from seeking or obtaining additional information beyond what was provided in the record, already provided by non-U.S. government entities, such as UNHCR or the Resettlement Support Center.

With respect to country of origin information (COI), rather than using COI to inform their interviews and adjudications, USCIS, under the Biden administration, trained refugee officers that for certain populations, they could rely on COI “profiles” ( e.g., “Venezuelans who oppose the government of Venezuela”) to establish various elements of refugee eligibility once an alien indicated they were part of a group of individuals for which COI supported a finding of well-founded fear. Officers shifted from individualized, more detailed assessments of refugee eligibility to confining interviews to review of the Form I-590 and an alien's affirmation of belonging to a designated group ( e.g., Rohingya), rather than exploring and evaluating an alien's unique experiences of past persecution or fears. In doing so, they bypassed in-depth interviews exploring an alien's background, experiences of past persecution in their home country, affiliations and relationships, if the alien in fact had a well-founded fear of future persecution in their home country, and other relevant details.

In 2017, President Trump issued Executive Order 13769 , Protecting the Nation from Foreign Terrorist Entry into the United States, restricting entry to the U.S. by certain foreign nationals and temporarily suspending the USRAP. [ 35 ]

During this suspension of refugee processing agencies were directed to review and strengthen vetting procedures. As a result of the review, USCIS clarified and confirmed that as a matter of policy, officers interviewing refugee applicants were required to elicit sufficient information to make a determination on both the past persecution and well-founded fear of future persecution claims. Gathering testimony on both past persecution and well-founded fear ensures a thorough and accurate evaluation of the applicant's eligibility and prevents overlooking critical facts that could substantiate, or call into question, their claim. For example, thorough elicitation of testimony regarding past and future harm may help identify inconsistencies and potential fraud by allowing adjudicators to probe the alien's narrative for credibility by ensuring it is internally consistent and consistent with statements the alien may have provided to processing partners prior to interview. Most importantly, it requires officers to probe more thoroughly into an applicant's background and experiences, helping to establish his or her identity, and further ensure that the correct decision is made in his or her case. Although eliciting testimony about both past persecution and well-founded fear helps develop a fuller picture of the alien and better assess eligibility—ensuring that protection is granted to those who genuinely qualify under the law—during the Biden administration this policy was rescinded. Refugee officers were no longer required to elicit testimony on both past persecution and well-founded fear claims, and were instead instructed to only pursue one or the other, once one had been established, precluding opportunities to identify critical information and concerns related to an alien's eligibility.

In addition to the relaxed requirements for principal refugee applicants, USCIS changed policies regarding derivative applicants. The first Trump administration issued guidance emphasizing the importance of eliciting testimony from derivative I-590 applicants apart from the principal refugee applicant to further explore potential national security, identity, inadmissibility, and credibility issues. However, USCIS subsequently rescinded this guidance under the Biden administration and provided refugee officers the sole discretion on when to interview derivative applicants separately. The purpose of this change was to reduce the amount of questions and time spent with derivatives in an interview, thus not thoroughly vetting and identifying potential issues of all members of a case who, upon case approval, were eligible to travel to the United States as refugees along with the principal applicant.

Compounding the issue, marriage guidance under the previous administration relaxed the criteria for adding a derivative spouse to a case. Although intended to accommodate couples who genuinely acted as spouses but could not formalize their union due to local restrictions, the standards were misapplied, allowing individuals with minimal or short-term connections to be classified as spouses and included on cases. This practice, combined with lowered interview standards and increasingly brief, less detailed case reviews in the name of streamlining, increased the risk of approving applicants with only tenuous relationships with the principal applicant.

In parallel with this minimized focus on eliciting substantive information to comprehensively understand an alien's background and identify potential issues of concern, the increased interview quotas made it more difficult for officers to explore important issues, fully probe the alien's credibility, and still meet their productivity expectations. During the first Trump administration, USCIS reduced the number of refugee interviews conducted per day per officer for certain cases to allow for further exploration of potential national security, inadmissibility, and credibility issues at interviews for refugee adjudications. Notwithstanding, USCIS under the Biden administration, in their effort to streamline interviews and increase the volume of refugee cases that could be processed, increased the number of cases an officer was expected to interview and adjudicate in a day for certain cases, again pressuring officers to at times scale back interviews to comply with the expectations.

This shift away from in-depth, thorough interviews in order to streamline and expedite admission of aliens to the United States as refugees shut down important lines of questioning to identify potential national security, public safety, and other concerns to accurately assess eligibility, illustrating the program's emphasis on the volume of refugee case completions rather than the quality of interviews or the integrity of
( printed page 65083)

adjudications. Refugee officers potentially missed vital information that could impact an applicant's eligibility, including issues related to fraud, public safety, and national security, and discretionary factors. USCIS, under the Biden administration, failed to fulfill its responsibility to ensure that its officers thoroughly assessed applicants, potentially resulting in an influx of ineligible aliens into the country that may pose a risk to the national interests of the United States.

Moreover, USCIS under the Biden administration decreased requirements for supervisory review of refugee cases by only requiring review of the assessment in lieu of reviewing the entire case contents. This limited supervisor oversight to ensure cases were thoroughly and accurately adjudicated, increased the risk that important information about an alien was overlooked.

An overarching desire to approve as many refugee cases as possible to meet the refugee ceiling set by the Biden administration contributed to a culture in which the expectation appeared to be to approve cases, even where egregious concerns may have existed. For instance, in one processing location, a number of aliens identified as having defrauded the U.S. government or submitting fraudulent documentation were found inadmissible pursuant to the INA provisions related to fraud and misrepresentation. Despite clear evidence of misrepresentation, including falsification of identity and key information relevant to their access to the USRAP, USCIS almost universally approved waivers of the misrepresentation or fraud. This pattern demonstrates a troubling disregard for the integrity of the refugee program, as individuals who had already demonstrated a willingness to engage in fraud and misrepresentation of their identities to U.S. government officials, were nonetheless permitted to proceed with resettlement to the United States, undermining both the security and credibility of the admissions process.

The persistent presence of individuals, both in the United States and overseas, attempting to exploit and defraud the U.S. humanitarian programs, poses risks to national security, public safety, and the integrity of the U.S. immigration system. Historically, DHS and State have identified, through investigations, fraud concerns among the special humanitarian access categories. For example, in January 2021, DHS and State suspended the Iraqi Direct Access P-2 Program, following an extensive investigation carried out by the State Diplomatic Security Service and the DHS Office of the Inspector General, which uncovered a fraud scheme related to the program. [ 36 ]
According to the indictment and statement of facts agreed to by one of the three defendants in the criminal case against the individuals:

from approximately February 2016 until at least April 2019, the three defendants, led by Abduljabbar, conspired to steal U.S. government records related to hundreds of USRAP applications . . . As part of their duties, both defendants had access to . . . a database containing sensitive, non-public information about refugee applicants and their family members, as well as the results of security checks and internal assessments by U.S. officials regarding applications. [ 37 ]

With regard to properly establishing familial relationships in the refugee P-3 family reunification program, this program was also temporarily suspended when evidence revealed widespread fraud. [ 38 ]

State previously indicated “[w]e were . . .only able to confirm all claimed biological relationships in fewer than 20% of cases (family units). In the remaining cases, at least one negative result (fraudulent relationship) was identified, or the individuals refused to be tested.”  [ 39 ]
Combined with recent policies that have lowered standards across the refugee program, these factors have created significant challenges and highlight the urgent need for this regulation.

An alarming illustration of the potentially dangerous impact of relaxed screening of the refugee population under the Biden administration occurred in the fall of 2024. CBP officers determined that several Venezuelan nationals who USCIS interviewed and approved for refugee classification were inadmissible and denied the aliens refugee status and entry at the border after the officers discovered tattoos associated with the deadly Tren de Aragua gang, a group designated as a Foreign Terrorist Organization in 2025. [ 40 ]

In some of these cases, refugee officers did not inquire about tattoos during their adjudications while the officers in others did not recognize that the tattoos the officers asked about were suggestive of gang membership, association, or affiliation. [ 41 ]

Following this incident, USCIS completed a review of records of over 14,500 cases (over 31,000 aliens) from Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Venezuela who were admitted to the United States as refugees between 2021 and 2024. The review identified over 1,500 cases (over 3,700 aliens) with indicators of potential public safety concerns. These cases included applicants with possible indicia of gang membership, association, or affiliation, including but not limited to tattoos associated with gangs, applicants romantically linked to gang members, medical records contradicting testimony from applicants regarding tattoos or drug use, prior criminal convictions, and/or evidence of a relationship with a suspected or confirmed gang member ( e.g., platonic, familial, household, linked cases). Each case presenting such indicia should have been appropriately evaluated on a case-by-case basis to ensure that cases presenting a public safety or national security risk would be found inadmissible, denied entry at the border, and thus denied refugee status.
## D. Recent Actions by President Trump and DHS To Reinvigorate Refugee Screening and Integrity of the Refugee Program
On January 20, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order (E.O.) 14161, Protecting the United States From Foreign Terrorists and Other National Security and Public Safety Threats. [ 42 ]
This order is intended to safeguard U.S. citizens from aliens who may seek to commit terrorist acts, pose threats to
( printed page 65084)

national security, promote hateful ideologies, or exploit immigration laws for malicious purposes. E.O. 14161 underscores the importance of vigilance during the visa issuance process to ensure that individuals approved for admission into the United States do not intend to harm Americans or compromise U.S. national interests.

Section 3(B) of E.O. 14161 further mandates that “sufficient safeguards are in place to prevent any refugee or stateless individual from being admitted to the United States without undergoing stringent identification beyond that required of any other alien seeking admission or entry to the United States[.]”  [ 43 ]
In the E.O. 14163 , Realigning the United States Refugee Admissions Program, [ 44 ]

President Trump also stated that suspended entry into the United States of refugees under the USRAP was due to the United States being inundated with record levels of migration that are detrimental to the interests of the United States. [ 45 ]

The President explained that the United States was unable to absorb large numbers of refugees into its communities without compromising resources for Americans, protecting safety and security, and ensuring appropriate assimilation of refugees. Id.

Consistent with the E.O., prioritizing public safety and national security is of the utmost importance to DHS. Pursuant to the President's direction in E.O. 14163 , Realigning the United States Refugee Admissions Program, DHS suspended decisions on applications for refugee classification as well as entry into the United States of refugees under the USRAP on January 20, 2025, to protect the safety and security of the American people and uphold a lawful and orderly U.S. immigration system. The USRAP is currently suspended because the Biden Administration prioritized expediency and admissions over quality screening and evaluation of refugee applicants' eligibility. During this suspension, the USRAP is only admitting refugees on a case-by-case basis, in the discretion of the Secretary of State and the Secretary of Homeland Security, and since the start of the FY 2026, in accordance with the Presidential Determination on Refugee Admissions for FY 2026,” but only so long as [the Secretaries] determine that the entry of such aliens as refugees is in the national interest and does not pose a threat to the security or welfare of the United States.”  [ 46 ]

To address and combat potential fallout from the lax refugee processing during the Biden administration, USCIS launched Operation Post-Admission Refugee Reverification and Integrity Strengthening (Operation PARRIS), to review background checks, conduct reinterviews, and review refugee claims based on the available record. [ 47 ]

Upon review and scrutiny of underlying refugee claims for aliens admitted to the United States as refugees, USCIS determined the record for a number of these aliens did not support the finding that the alien met the refugee definition at the time of admission and he or she required follow-up questioning. USCIS began issuing NOITs to those under this review who were found to not have met the definition of a refugee at the time of admission.

As noted above, on January 9, 2026, DHS announced the launch of Operation PARRIS, a sweeping initiative first centered in Minnesota to reexamine thousands of refugee cases through new background checks and intensive verification of refugee claims. [ 48 ]

In this announcement, DHS asserted it will “not stand idly by as the U.S. immigration system is weaponized by those seeking to defraud the American people. American citizens and the rule of law come first, always.”  [ 49 ]

Operation PARRIS is part of a broader strategy to implement enhanced screening standards under E.O. 14161 . These directives require federal agencies to identify and implement new vetting enhancements to safeguard the nation from terrorists and other public safety threats. [ 50 ]

In Operation PARRIS, DHS is identifying and referring cases of fraud, national security and public safety concerns, and other criminal activity to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). An initial review of a select subset of cases revealed a persistent issue of inconsistency in interview quality. While some interviews were thorough and well-conducted, others were lacking. These interviews are characterized by minimal questioning, little to no appropriate follow-up questioning, and insufficient inquiry into critical matters such as grounds of inadmissibility, including terrorism-related grounds leading to refugee admissions of aliens whose identities and backgrounds were not properly confirmed. Aliens with unknown identity and background pose risks to U.S. national security.

On December 5, 2025, USCIS established the USCIS Vetting Center, a specialized unit designed to screen out terrorists, criminal aliens, and other foreign nationals who pose potential threats to public safety, have committed fraud, or committed other crimes. [ 51 ]

Since its creation, the USCIS Vetting Center has dedicated a task force to conduct review of certain refugee cases previously approved under the Biden administration. The findings of this task force underscore the deficiencies and risks to public safety and national security associated with the prior administration's approach to the refugee program, including insufficient vetting and inadequate assessment of applicants' identities, backgrounds, associations, and eligibility for refugee status. For instance, a review of a resettled Ethiopian refugee case revealed inconsistencies and other credibility issues regarding the applicant's involvement with and financial support for the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF), a group that met the definition of a Tier III terrorist group at the time of the applicant's involvement, as well as his father's affiliation with the OLF. The refugee status was subsequently terminated. Additional cases reviewed by the task force involved resettled refugees who misrepresented material facts about their identities and family members, such as providing inconsistent marriage information between their I-590 and I-485 forms, and failing to disclose spouses or children during the I-590 interview while later reporting them on the I-485. Through enhanced vetting procedures implemented under the current administration, the task force also identified cases of refugees promoting hateful and violent rhetoric or supporting terrorist organizations on their social media profiles.
## IV. Discussion of Interim Final Rule
Previous administrations' prioritization of the admissions of large numbers of refugees over homeland
( printed page 65085)

security blatantly overlooked essential components of eligibility and put at risk the national security, public safety and other interests of the U.S. citizenry. Safeguarding national security and public safety remains the foremost priority of the country's immigration programs, taking precedence over numerical admission targets. The agency stands committed to conducting rigorous vetting of all aliens and to the detection and prevention of fraud and other serious threats, ensuring the safety of all Americans prior to admission of an alien to the United States.

Accordingly, this IFR shortens the amount of time that refugees are provided to respond to a NOIT in order to ensure that terminations of refugee status can occur as expeditiously as possible to protect national security and public safety, given the risks created by the deficient vetting described above in Section III.C. Under this IFR, refugees will continue to receive a NOIT, which will specify DHS's intent to terminate their refugee status based on a determination that they did not meet the refugee definition at the time of admission. DHS will provide the specific reason or reasons why USCIS found the refugee failed to meet the refugee definition at the time of admission ( e.g., failure to establish that past harm experienced was serious enough to rise to the level of persecution, a determination that the alien's harm was not on account of a protected ground, failure to provide credible testimony as to any or all of the elements of the refugee definition, etc.). However, this rule will provide such aliens with ten days (rather than 30 days) to respond (provide documentary evidence or indicate a desire to provide oral evidence) if they choose. If the deadline to reply to the NOIT passes without a response, the refugee is considered to have forfeited his or her right to rebut the allegations in the NOIT, and DHS will terminate his or her refugee status.
By regulation, the response period begins either upon personal service of the NOIT directly to the alien or, if sent by mail, upon mailing of the NOIT. [ 52 ]
When calculating the response deadline, all days, including Saturdays, Sundays, and federal holidays, are counted. [ 53 ]
However, if the final day falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or federal holiday, the deadline is extended to the next business day. [ 54 ]
Per 8 CFR 103.8(b) , if the notice is served by mail, three days are added to the response period, with service considered complete on the date the notice is mailed.

DHS's foremost priority is the safety and security of American citizens and residents. At the same time, DHS is committed to ensuring that refugees who receive a NOIT are afforded a meaningful opportunity to respond or provide a rebuttal. To enhance mail service reliability and afford refugees the full response period, DHS will utilize express delivery service providers, which guarantee a three-day delivery window and offer tracking and confirmation of both the NOIT's departure from DHS custody and its delivery to the recipient. [ 55 ]

This approach ensures that refugees receive their NOIT promptly and can exercise their right to respond. The NOIT will be dated on the day it is mailed, and the 10-day response period for the refugee will begin from that date. If the refugee wishes to request an opportunity to provide oral testimony in lieu of responding to each point or points in the NOIT, such a request would be considered a timely response by DHS. As explained above, in accordance with 8 CFR 103.8(b) , when a notice is served by mail, three additional days are added to the response period, with service considered complete on the date the notice is mailed. Therefore, applicants who are mailed notices are afforded a total of 13 days to respond, accounting for this regulatory provision.

Reducing the 30-day response timeframe for NOITs issued in refugee terminations to a 10-day response timeframe allows DHS to take swifter action in cases where aliens did not meet the definition of a refugee when admitted to the United States. USCIS needs the ability to terminate refugee status in such cases in order to more quickly begin the removal process for aliens who should never have been admitted to the United States as refugees in the first place, including aliens similarly situated to those discussed above in Section III.C, who also pose a national security or public safety risk. While termination of refugee status is not a precondition for initiation of removal proceedings, the termination of refugee status gives DHS a statutory basis for removal, and in some cases, no other removal grounds apply, so this termination is needed. [ 56 ]

Accordingly, promptly terminating refugee status in cases where the alien was clearly ineligible at the time of admission facilitates DHS's ability to process the alien for removal under sections 235, 240, and 241 of the INA, and to remove the alien if they do not qualify for relief from removal.

More broadly, timely termination of their refugee status is critical to the integrity of the country's immigration programs, considering the risks they may pose to the United States. As USCIS continues to encounter aliens admitted as refugees who did not meet the definition of refugee at the time of admission, termination of refugee status in as prompt and efficient manner as possible ensures USCIS can best protect the safety and security of Americans and continue complying with E.O.s 14161 and 14163. By shortening the 30-day period for an alien to respond to a NOIT to 10 days, USCIS is exercising its authority to expeditiously terminate the status of refugees who did not meet the refugee definition at the time of their admission to the United States. Streamlining the termination process additionally ensures that ineligible aliens who were erroneously allowed to enter the United States as refugees lose their authorization to work in as timely a manner as possible since termination of refugee status also results in termination of employment authorization.

DHS believes that reducing the NOIT response period from 30 days to 10 days maintains adequate procedural safeguards for aliens by affording them an opportunity to respond to the NOIT while also balancing the government's interests in national security and public safety and in protecting the integrity of the refugee program. The NOIT will inform the alien the basis for termination and explain that they may submit evidence to contest termination, and/or request an interview. An alien does not need to submit evidence or a full response within the 10 days, and may instead opt for an interview, but must make the interview request to USCIS within the response period.
( printed page 65086)

Aliens who receive a NOIT under the proposed process therefore will continue to receive a meaningful opportunity to respond to the allegations in the notice—the alien can submit a written response to the NOIT within the deadline and/or request an interview with USCIS where their refugee claim can be heard. The abbreviated time period to respond to the NOIT will in turn allow the government to more efficiently process cases where aliens did not meet the refugee definition at the time of admission to the United States, and who were from the outset, never eligible for the benefit they received. Instead of waiting 30 days for an alien to respond to a NOIT before scheduling an interview if requested by the alien or taking other action, this rule will allow USCIS to act as soon as 10 days after service of the NOIT. For aliens who do not respond timely, the 10-day response period will allow USCIS to finalize termination much more quickly. Furthermore, each alien whose refugee status is terminated will be processed under INA sections 235, 240, or 241 and may seek other forms of relief or protection from removal as permitted in those proceedings. For example, aliens in section 240 removal proceedings may seek other forms of relief in a hearing before an immigration judge where the interests of the U.S. Government are properly represented by an attorney from the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Office of the Principal Legal Advisor (OPLA).

The regulatory amendment being made in this IFR is clearly authorized by INA 207(c)(4), 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(4) , which gives discretion to the Secretary to “prescribe” regulations governing termination of aliens who were “not in fact a refugee within the meaning of section 101(a)(42) . . . at the time of the alien's admission.”
## V. Statutory and Regulatory Requirements
## A. Administrative Procedures Act (APA)

DHS is issuing this IFR without prior notice or public procedure because DHS is invoking the “good cause” and foreign affairs exceptions of the APA. See 5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1) , (b)(B). For the same reasons, a delayed effective date of no less than 30 days is not required under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3) . DHS has also considered potential reliance interests and discusses them below.
## a. Good Cause

An agency may forgo notice-and-comment rulemaking and a delayed effective date when the agency “for good cause finds . . . that notice and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.” See 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B) . Likewise, section 553(d)'s requirement of 30-day advance publication may be waived by the agency for good cause found and published with the rule. See 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3) .

The “impracticable” prong of the good cause exception excuses notice and comment in emergency situations, or where the delay caused by the APA's notice-and-comment procedures would result in serious harm to life, property, or an immediate threat to public safety. [ 57 ]
